title: Work out harder facts with doubling/halving, annexing zeros and the distributive property

lesson.title: Break It Apart: Easy Ways to Get the Tricky Facts

steps.say: You already know your fives, your threes and your tens really well. So when a tricky fact like six times eight pops up, we do not have to guess — we can break it into pieces we already know.

Here is six rows of eight. Six is just five plus one, so I can slice the picture into a five-row piece and a one-row piece. The big shaded piece is five times eight, which is forty. The leftover row is one more eight. Forty plus eight is forty-eight.

visual.caption: Six rows of eight, sliced into five rows (40) plus one more row (8)

steps.say: There is a second easy path: doubling. Three times eight is twenty-four, and six is double three, so six times eight is double twenty-four. Double twenty-four is forty-eight. Same answer — nice, that means we got it right.

visual.caption: Three rows of eight is 24; six rows is double that, 48

steps.say: Now the zero trick. Say hockey pucks cost eighty dollars for a team pack and you buy six packs. Six times eight is forty-eight, and because we are counting eights of ten, the answer is forty-eight tens — that is four hundred eighty dollars. Multiply the easy fact first, then stick the zero on.

Here is the slip lots of kids make. They break six into five plus one, get forty, then add only one and say forty-one. But look at that leftover row — it is a whole row of eight squares, not one square. The one means one more group of eight. So it is forty plus eight, forty-eight.

visual.caption: The leftover row holds eight squares, not one

steps.say: So whenever a fact feels hard, break it into friendly pieces, or double an easier fact, and handle the zeros last.

lesson.answer: Break the tricky fact into friendly pieces you already know, add them up, then annex the zeros.

practice.question: A hockey puck at the Burnaby sports shop costs eight dollars. Coach buys seven pucks. Break seven into five plus two: work out five times eight, then two times eight, then add them. What is the total? Then try the bigger one — if each puck cost eighty dollars instead, what would seven pucks cost?
practice.answer: Five times eight is forty, and two times eight is sixteen. Forty plus sixteen is fifty-six, so seven pucks cost 56 dollars. At eighty dollars each: seven times eight is fifty-six, so seven times eighty is 560 dollars.
